channel.title: AI GridWatch Blog
channel.description: Analysis and explainers on data center development, grid impact, and community advocacy.

item.title: Anthropic Went Public With $900 Billion in Compute Commitments. Here Are the Promises It Made to the Towns That Host It.
item.description: Anthropic began trading on Nov. 19. Its prospectus discloses about $900.9 billion in commitments, nearly all for compute and data centers, and repeats a pledge to cover electricity price increases its data centers cause. The company has also published commitments on tax incentives, NDAs and community benefit agreements. The prospectus names no sites. One landlord's filing does, in Navarro County, Texas, and its terms are worth reading against the pledges.

item.title: 434 House Races Have a Winner. Only 91 of Them Ever Said Anything Specific About Data Centers.
item.description: Our House tracker now records a result for every one of the 440 seats on the ballot: 434 winners and six races still in a recount or runoff. Ninety-one winners have a documented position on data centers. Another 228 are on the record only for one near-unanimous vote. The rest have said nothing we could find, including the new member for the South Jersey district where Vineland sits. What the results show, where they cut against the easy story, and how to look up your own district.

item.title: Nvidia Is Guaranteeing $105 Billion for One Data Center Campus in Pike County, Ohio
item.description: Nvidia's quarterly filing on Nov. 17 shows the chipmaker standing behind $118 billion in guarantees for other companies' data centers. $105 billion of it backs a single site: the PORTS-Pike campus on the old uranium enrichment plant in Pike County, Ohio. What the filing says, what was promised to the county in August, and the state approvals that are still ahead.

item.title: Five Governors-Elect Promised a Data Center Pause. Here Is What a Governor Can Actually Do.
item.description: Of 34 winning candidates for governor, 32 backed tighter rules on data centers and 12 backed a ban or moratorium, according to a tally cited by the Associated Press. The pledges are real. So are the limits: a governor cannot repeal a tax break alone, cannot freeze a permit already issued, and an executive-order pause may not survive a lawsuit. A state-by-state read of what was promised and which lever it depends on.

item.title: Nine Senate Seats Flipped. Here Is What the Winners Put in Writing About Data Centers.
item.description: All 35 Senate races on the 2026 ballot now have a called winner. Thirteen of those winners left a documented position on data centers during the campaign, and twelve of the thirteen promised some version of the same thing: data centers pay their own way. This post lists who promised what, with the source for each, and what none of it guarantees.

item.title: Week in Review: Minneapolis Passes Data Center Rules But Not a Ban, Oakland Extends Its Moratorium to 2027, and a Third Lawsuit Hits OpenAI's Georgia Project
item.description: Eight cities and counties landed in eight different places on the spectrum from outright ban to negotiated settlement this week. Minneapolis passed new data center rules but not the ban some residents wanted; Oakland extended its moratorium through 2027; Springfield, Missouri's moratorium survived a developer's court challenge; and a third lawsuit, this one alleging racketeering, hit OpenAI's Project Camellia in Effingham County, Georgia. In North Texas, Fort Worth is still weighing a 90-day pause while neighboring Westlake already settled its way to a cleared project. Plus: a 800-signature petition in Bow, New Hampshire, a second failed moratorium vote in Aurora, Colorado, and a push to block an air permit in South Brunswick, New Jersey.

item.title: Week in Review: Data Centers Lose Nearly Every Ballot Measure Nationwide, Georgia Flips Its Utility Board, and OpenAI Launches a Post-Election Charm Offensive
item.description: In Tuesday's elections, voters decided data-center ballot measures in roughly ten states and 41 local contests — the industry won one. Ohio's wave of local bans swept through Election Day and cost Vantage Data Centers a project in Oregon, Ohio; Georgia voters flipped control of the state's Public Service Commission; and Texas elected a governor who says she'll keep the state's data center moratorium going. OpenAI responded with a new policy framework promising more local input and a pledge to cover its own power costs. Plus: Bernie Sanders wants a national moratorium, and fresh bans in Maine, Connecticut and New Jersey.

item.title: Week in Review: Charlotte Extends Its Data Center Pause to 2027, Aurora Fails to Ban Them Twice, and a Federal Judge Keeps a Pollution Suit Against Elon Musk's xAI Alive
item.description: Charlotte's City Council unanimously extended its data center moratorium by 11 months, to October 2027, while Aurora, Colorado failed for the second time in two weeks to even bring a moratorium up for a vote, falling short of the supermajority its own rules require. Davidson County, North Carolina and San Antonio, Texas both rejected moratoriums in favor of permanent rules and case-by-case council approval instead, Pittsburg, California adopted a 45-day pause with a disputed scope, and Oklahoma City approved a rezoning under its own moratorium because the application beat the deadline. Plus: a federal judge refuses to let the Trump administration dismiss the NAACP's Clean Air Act lawsuit against Elon Musk's xAI, and three more fights move in Pennsylvania, Virginia and Iowa.

item.title: Salix, Iowa Says It Has No Data Center Moratorium. It Just Signed a Cost Deal With Google.
item.description: On Oct. 14 the Salix, Iowa council voted 3-2 to state that no data center moratorium exists, then 3-2 to approve an agreement under which Google pays up to $150,000 for the city's outside advisors. The land has not been sold and no rezoning has been filed. Here is what the agreement does and does not say.

item.title: Week in Review: Oregon's Governor Pauses Data Center Permits Statewide, Milwaukee Bans New Ones for a Year, and a $3 Billion Massachusetts Project Dies on a Technicality
item.description: Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek ordered state regulators to stop issuing air and water permits for new data centers until mid-2027, and Milwaukee's Common Council unanimously passed its own one-year moratorium. In Texas, Hood County commissioners rejected a developer's settlement offer and permit appeal despite an explicit threat of a lawsuit, while in Massachusetts, a Planning Board quietly killed a $3-4 billion data center campus by refusing to extend a permit the developer let lapse. Plus: Memphis and Shelby County both advance competing moratorium ordinances, a month-old New Jersey diesel spill still hasn't drawn a fine, and West Virginia's governor strikes a deal to relocate a rare 200-tree chestnut grove instead of clearing it.

item.title: Week in Review: San Francisco Bans Data Centers in the Birthplace of AI, Texas's Own Utility Regulator Sues to Keep Data Center Locations Secret, and Memphis's Moratorium Vote Ends in a Brawl
item.description: This week San Francisco and Oakland each passed 45-day data center moratoriums in the city where OpenAI, Anthropic, and most of the AI industry is headquartered, and Texas's own Public Utility Commission sued Attorney General Ken Paxton's office to keep data center location records secret. Memphis's council postponed its moratorium vote twice amid a meeting that ended in a physical altercation, Raleigh passed a six-month pause after activists asked for 32 months, Georgia and Virginia regulators cited data centers for environmental and permit violations, and a federal judge upheld Nashville's authority to pause a project near the city zoo. Plus: Denver7 counted nearly 500 U.S. communities that have now paused or banned data centers.

item.title: Developers Are Suing Towns That Ban Data Centers. Here Is What the Cases Say.
item.description: At least eight data center developers have filed lawsuits against local moratoriums and bans in 2026. One Texas county rescinded its moratorium within two weeks of being sued for $100 million. Others are fighting back. The cases are drawing a practical line between bans that hold and bans that fold.

item.title: Amazon Pledged $1 Billion to Data Center Communities. Here Is What the Number Actually Means.
item.description: AWS announced a $1 billion, five-year community investment program called Built Together alongside a promise to stop requiring NDAs from local governments. The headline is large. The math, measured against Amazon's own capital spending and the tax breaks it already claims, is not.

item.title: Three Southern Cities Let Their Data Center Moratoriums End. Here Is What They Wrote Instead.
item.description: In September, moratoriums in Augusta, Georgia, Birmingham, Alabama and Roswell, Georgia all came to an end. Each city replaced its pause with permanent rules, but the rules are not alike, and Augusta's passed by a single vote. What they cover, and what a resident can learn from them before their own town's pause runs out.

item.title: New Jersey Fined Vineland's Data Center $1.07 Million. The Order Gives It 45 Days, Not a Shutdown.
item.description: NJDEP's order against DataOne is five pages long, and it says more than the headlines about it. The $1,072,000 penalty covers 62 gas engines installed and run without permits. The company has 45 days to file permit applications, and the engines only have to stop if it misses that filing deadline. Here is what the order requires, what it leaves open, and what Vineland residents can check next.

item.title: Week in Review: New Jersey's Record Data Center Fine, Prince William County Ends By-Right Approval, and Palm Beach County Passes a Moratorium — Then Cuts Its Own Resident Task Force
item.description: This week New Jersey hit a Vineland data center with its largest-ever civil penalty over 62 unpermitted gas generators, Prince William County, Virginia ended by-right approval for new data centers countywide, and Texas's attorney general opened an investigation into hundreds of data centers that never answered a mandatory water-use survey. A Republican and a Democrat in Congress each introduced NDA-transparency bills the same week, Memphis-area residents filed two separate lawsuits against an xAI data center in one week, and Palm Beach County passed a year-long moratorium — then scrapped its own resident task force in favor of paid consultants. Plus: nine more communities paused or banned data centers in the past seven days.

item.title: Newsom Signed Seven Data Center Bills. None of Them Has a Threshold Yet.
item.description: On September 21, Governor Newsom signed seven data center bills into law -- the same package he blocked a year ago. The laws shift grid upgrade costs to operators, mandate water and energy disclosure, and strip a blanket environmental exemption. But every dollar figure and megawatt trigger is delegated to future CPUC rulemaking, with no filing deadline. Here is what each bill actually requires, what it leaves to regulators, and what a community can use right now.

item.title: Trump Announced an AI Force. The Same Week, His Own Pollster Said Data Centers Are a Losing Issue.
item.description: On September 19, President Trump announced an 'AI Force' modeled on the Space Force and promised an AI czar. Four days earlier, his own pollster told Republican candidates that unqualified support for data centers is 'a losing position.' The same weekend, Texas froze all data center environmental permits and California signed seven data center laws. What actually happened, and what it means for communities heading into a hearing.

item.title: Two Georgia Data Center Lawsuits in Five Days, and Neither One Argues the Project Is a Bad Idea
item.description: Residents in Statesboro and Effingham County, Georgia filed separate Superior Court challenges to data center decisions between September 17 and 21. One attacks a rezoning, the other attacks how a development authority kept OpenAI's deal quiet. Both lean on process rather than on whether a data center belongs there, and both started on a clock.

item.title: Climate Week Put Amazon's Texas Gas Plant on the Agenda. Its Developer Is Already Pitching the Next County.
item.description: During Climate Week NYC, Amazon workers and Bill McKibben pointed at the 35-turbine gas plant Amazon is financing in Pecos County, Texas. The same week, that plant's developer met Brewster County officials about a second off-grid data center and gas plant in the Glass Mountains. What a county in that position should know about the claims on both sides.
